name: Ad hominem
definition: Attacking the person making a claim instead of the claim itself, so the argument's merits are ignored.
example: You can't trust his budget proposal, he's been divorced twice.
not_to_be_confused_with: Pointing out a genuine conflict of interest that is relevant to the claim.

name: Straw man
definition: Misrepresenting an opponent's position as something weaker or more extreme, then refuting that version.
example: She wants stricter speed limits, so she wants everyone to drive at walking pace.
not_to_be_confused_with: Fairly summarising a view and then criticising it.

name: Appeal to authority
definition: Claiming something must be true because an authority or expert says so, without examining the actual evidence or their relevant expertise.
example: A famous actor says this investment is guaranteed to succeed, so it must be safe.
not_to_be_confused_with: Using the informed opinion of a qualified expert as relevant supporting evidence.

name: Appeal to popularity (Argumentum ad populum)
definition: Claiming something is true, correct, or good because many people believe it or do it.
example: Millions of people believe this rumour, so there must be something to it.
not_to_be_confused_with: Using popularity as evidence of a product's market demand.

name: False dilemma (False dichotomy)
definition: Presenting only two possible options when additional alternatives exist.
example: Either you support this policy or you don't care about the country.
not_to_be_confused_with: Identifying two genuinely mutually exclusive possibilities.

name: Slippery slope
definition: Claiming that a relatively small initial action will inevitably trigger a chain of increasingly extreme consequences without sufficient evidence.
example: If we allow students to submit one assignment late, soon nobody will ever meet a deadline.
not_to_be_confused_with: Demonstrating a plausible causal chain supported by evidence.

name: Hasty generalisation
definition: Drawing a broad conclusion from an insufficient or unrepresentative sample.
example: Two tourists from that country were rude to me, so everyone from there must be rude.
not_to_be_confused_with: Drawing a cautious conclusion from a sufficiently large and representative sample.

name: Post hoc ergo propter hoc
definition: Assuming that because one event happened after another, the first event must have caused the second.
example: I wore my lucky socks and then we won the match, so my socks caused the victory.
not_to_be_confused_with: Establishing causation through evidence, controlled experiments, or a credible causal mechanism.

name: Cum hoc ergo propter hoc
definition: Assuming that because two things occur together, one must cause the other.
example: Ice cream sales and drownings both increase in summer, so ice cream must cause drownings.
not_to_be_confused_with: Identifying a genuine causal relationship between correlated variables.

name: Begging the question (Circular reasoning)
definition: Using a conclusion as one of the premises supporting that same conclusion.
example: This law is just because it is the right law to have.
not_to_be_confused_with: Using an independently established premise to support a conclusion.

name: Red herring
definition: Introducing an irrelevant point to distract from the original argument or question.
example: Why are you questioning my spending? You should be grateful that I work so hard.
not_to_be_confused_with: Introducing genuinely relevant additional context.

name: Tu quoque
definition: Rejecting criticism by accusing the critic of behaving inconsistently with their own advice.
example: You tell me to stop smoking, but you used to smoke yourself, so your argument is invalid.
not_to_be_confused_with: Pointing out hypocrisy when the consistency or credibility of the speaker is genuinely relevant.

name: Appeal to ignorance (Argumentum ad ignorantiam)
definition: Claiming something is true because it has not been proven false, or false because it has not been proven true.
example: Nobody has proven that aliens haven't visited Earth, so they definitely have.
not_to_be_confused_with: Treating a lack of evidence as relevant when evidence would reasonably be expected to exist.

name: Appeal to emotion
definition: Using emotional reactions such as fear, pity, anger, or guilt instead of relevant evidence to establish a conclusion.
example: You must support this proposal, otherwise think of all the children who will suffer.
not_to_be_confused_with: Using emotional language to communicate the genuine human consequences of an argument.

name: Appeal to tradition
definition: Claiming something is correct or desirable simply because it has been done that way for a long time.
example: We've always taught history this way, so changing the curriculum would be wrong.
not_to_be_confused_with: Recognising that established practices may contain accumulated experience or useful knowledge.

name: Appeal to nature
definition: Assuming that something is good, safe, or morally right simply because it is natural, or bad because it is artificial.
example: This chemical is naturally occurring, so it cannot possibly be harmful.
not_to_be_confused_with: Evaluating natural and synthetic substances according to their actual properties and effects.

name: No true Scotsman
definition: Protecting a generalisation from counterexamples by arbitrarily redefining the category to exclude them.
example: No real environmentalist drives an SUV. Anyone who does isn't a real environmentalist.
not_to_be_confused_with: Using a clearly established definition to distinguish between different categories.

name: Moving the goalposts
definition: Changing the requirements for accepting an argument after the original requirements have already been satisfied.
example: You said one study would convince you. Here's the study. Well, one study isn't enough; I need ten.
not_to_be_confused_with: Requesting additional evidence when new information reveals a genuine weakness.

name: Equivocation
definition: Using a word or phrase with multiple meanings in different parts of an argument to create a misleading conclusion.
example: The sign says fine for parking here, so parking here must be excellent.
not_to_be_confused_with: Using words with different meanings when the distinction is clearly established.

name: False analogy
definition: Comparing two things that are insufficiently similar in relevant respects to support the conclusion.
example: Running a country is just like running a household, so national debt must be managed exactly like household debt.
not_to_be_confused_with: Using an analogy that highlights relevant similarities while acknowledging important differences.

name: Composition fallacy
definition: Assuming that what is true of individual parts must also be true of the whole.
example: Every player on the team is excellent, so the team must be unbeatable.
not_to_be_confused_with: Showing that individual properties genuinely combine to produce a property of the whole.

name: Division fallacy
definition: Assuming that what is true of a whole must also be true of each of its individual parts.
example: That university is wealthy, so every student attending it must be wealthy.
not_to_be_confused_with: Identifying properties that genuinely apply to both a whole and its components.

name: Cherry picking
definition: Selecting only evidence that supports a conclusion while ignoring relevant contradictory evidence.
example: This medicine worked for three people, so it is effective, ignoring the hundreds of unsuccessful cases.
not_to_be_confused_with: Focusing on a particular subset of evidence when the scope and selection criteria are justified.

name: Anecdotal fallacy
definition: Using a personal experience or isolated example as sufficient evidence to establish a general conclusion.
example: My grandfather smoked every day and lived to 95, so smoking can't be dangerous.
not_to_be_confused_with: Using personal experiences as illustrative examples alongside broader evidence.

name: Burden of proof reversal
definition: Demanding that someone else disprove a claim rather than providing evidence for the claim being made.
example: Prove that my invisible dragon doesn't exist.
not_to_be_confused_with: Asking someone to justify a claim they have already made.

name: Special pleading
definition: Applying a standard or rule inconsistently by inventing an exception for a particular case without sufficient justification.
example: Rules against lying apply to everyone except me, because my intentions are always good.
not_to_be_confused_with: Recognising a legitimate exception supported by relevant differences.

name: Genetic fallacy
definition: Accepting or rejecting a claim based solely on its origin or source rather than evaluating its merits.
example: That idea came from a politician, so it must be wrong.
not_to_be_confused_with: Considering the origin of information when it provides relevant evidence about its reliability.

name: Guilt by association
definition: Discrediting an individual or argument by associating it with a person or group considered undesirable.
example: That scientist once worked with a controversial organisation, so none of their research can be trusted.
not_to_be_confused_with: Identifying a demonstrable shared interest, collaboration, or conflict that is relevant to the argument.

name: Middle ground fallacy
definition: Assuming that a compromise between two opposing positions must be correct simply because it lies between them.
example: One person says the Earth is round and another says it is flat, so the truth must be somewhere in between.
not_to_be_confused_with: Finding a reasonable compromise when both positions have valid considerations.

name: Texas sharpshooter fallacy
definition: Selecting patterns or clusters from random data after the fact and presenting them as evidence of a meaningful relationship.
example: A company highlights three successful predictions from hundreds of random guesses and claims its system is remarkably accurate.
not_to_be_confused_with: Testing a predicted pattern against independent data.

name: False cause
definition: Incorrectly identifying a causal relationship between events without sufficient evidence.
example: The economy improved after the new mayor took office, so the mayor must have caused the improvement.
not_to_be_confused_with: Establishing causation using appropriate evidence while accounting for alternative explanations.

name: Loaded question
definition: Asking a question that contains an unproven assumption, making any straightforward answer appear to concede that assumption.
example: Have you stopped cheating on your exams?
not_to_be_confused_with: Asking a direct question based on facts that have already been established.

name: Complex question fallacy
definition: Combining multiple questions or assumptions into one question so that answering it appears to accept all of them.
example: Why are you dishonest and unwilling to admit your mistakes?
not_to_be_confused_with: Asking multiple related questions after establishing their individual premises.

name: Argument from consequences
definition: Claiming that a proposition must be true or false because its consequences would be desirable or undesirable.
example: Climate change cannot be real because that would mean we need to change our lifestyles.
not_to_be_confused_with: Evaluating the practical consequences of accepting a proposition separately from its truth.

name: Appeal to wealth (Argumentum ad crumenam)
definition: Assuming that a wealthy person must be correct because of their financial success.
example: He's a billionaire, so his opinions on economics must be right.
not_to_be_confused_with: Considering someone's financial experience when it is directly relevant to a discussion.

name: Appeal to poverty (Argumentum ad lazarum)
definition: Assuming that a poor person must be more honest, virtuous, or correct because they are poor.
example: She has very little money, so she must be more trustworthy than a wealthy politician.
not_to_be_confused_with: Considering how financial circumstances may affect someone's experiences or interests.

name: Kettle logic
definition: Using multiple contradictory arguments to defend the same conclusion, as though all could be true simultaneously.
example: I never borrowed your car. Even if I did, I returned it. And besides, it was already damaged.
not_to_be_confused_with: Offering several compatible alternative explanations or defences.

name: Nirvana fallacy
definition: Rejecting a realistic solution because it is imperfect when compared with an impossible or ideal alternative.
example: Seatbelts don't prevent every road death, so there's no point wearing them.
not_to_be_confused_with: Criticising a solution because its real-world limitations make it ineffective or unsuitable.

name: Motte-and-bailey fallacy
definition: Making a controversial or extreme claim, then retreating to a much more defensible but weaker claim when challenged, before later returning to the original position.
example: Social media is destroying society. I only meant that social media can sometimes have negative effects. So clearly, it's destroying society.
not_to_be_confused_with: Clarifying an ambiguous statement or genuinely revising a position after criticism.
